project_scope.note: Cedar elm is the canonical elm anchor; Celtis references are used as the high-value family comparison.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start at leaf venation: local elms have pinnate venation with many lateral veins running toward serrated teeth, often with an asymmetric base.
family_diagnostics.leaves: Alternate simple distichous leaves with stipules; bases often conspicuously oblique.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Ulmus makes a dry winged samara.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: The fastest local split is elm pinnate venation + samara versus hackberry 3-basal-vein pattern + drupe.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → high-value structure → reproductive confirmation → tie-breaker
visual_lesson.intro: Elm identification gets much easier when you combine leaf venation with fruit, twig wings and season. First separate Ulmus samaras from Celtis drupes and Planera's warty fruit. Inside Ulmus, use twig wings + node behavior + reproductive season before trusting leaf shape.

steps.title: 1 · Cedar elm leaf + samara
steps.look_for: Many lateral veins running from the midrib toward the serrated margin, plus dry winged samaras.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the core local Ulmus pattern.

steps.title: 2 · Trace cedar elm leaf veins and serrations
steps.look_for: Follow the midrib, side veins and finely serrated edges of the small leaves. This is a leaf detail image, NOT the whole tree.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows the venation and leaf edge clearly without claiming this photo illustrates the entire tree.

steps.title: 3 · Hackberry tie-breaker
steps.look_for: Three strong primary veins arising near the leaf base.
steps.why_it_matters: That basal three-vein pattern strongly favors Celtis over Ulmus.

steps.title: 4 · Fruit seals the split
steps.look_for: A fleshy drupe rather than a dry samara.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit + venation makes elm-versus-hackberry much safer.

steps.title: 5 · Winged elm leaf: corky-wing comparison still missing
steps.look_for: Pointed serrated leaves from a winged elm. For corky nodes, no confidently verified matched twig macro is yet available; both winged elm and cedar elm can have corky wings.
steps.why_it_matters: Prevents the most important local false shortcut: 'corky wings = winged elm.'

steps.title: 6 · Chinese elm bark is the non-native giveaway
steps.look_for: Mottled exfoliating tan, gray and orange bark with small glossy leaves.
steps.why_it_matters: Separates a common planted/naturalized introduced elm from the native Central Texas elms.

comparisons.title: Elm vs hackberry
comparisons.rule: Ulmus = many pinnate side veins + samara. Celtis = strong basal 3-vein pattern + fleshy drupe.

comparisons.title: Winged elm vs cedar elm
comparisons.rule: Both may have corky wings. U. alata usually ends wings at nodes and fruits in spring; U. crassifolia often carries corky ridges around nodes and fruits in fall.

comparisons.title: Native elm vs Chinese elm
comparisons.rule: Chinese elm = exfoliating lacebark + smoother glossy small leaves + fall reproduction; keep it excluded from native totals.

visual_lesson.caveat: Hackberries are now Cannabaceae in modern classification; they remain here only as the most useful elm comparison.

family_confusion_polish.look_here_first: Ulmus: pinnate leaf veins and winged samaras. Planera: elm-like leaves but stalked warty non-samara fruits. Compare Celtis (three strong basal veins, drupe).

comparison_matrix.leaf: Numerous pinnate lateral veins; asymmetrical leaf base

family_confusion_polish.exceptions: Do not require winged fruit for every Ulmaceae: Planera lacks an elm-like samara. Celtis was historically treated with elms but belongs to Cannabaceae.
